Six-point demand: Medical technologists, pharmacists form human chain
2024-11-20T18:58:45+06:00 | Star Digital Report
https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/six-point-demand-medical-technologists-pharmacists-form-human-chain-3757541

Medical technologists and pharmacists from 20 medical colleges and healthcare institutions staged a human chain today, pressing for their six-point demand, including the establishment of a dedicated government directorate for their professions.

The protest, organised by the National Anti-Discrimination Medical Technologist and Pharmacist Council, was held from 10:00am to 11:00am at institutions such as Dhaka Medical College, Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital, Sir Salimullah Medical College Mitford Hospital, Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University, and Mugda Medical College.

With the banner of the "National Anti-Discrimination Medical Technologist and Pharmacist Council," protesters carried placards with messages such as "Pharmacists are essential for drug formulation" and "Recruit medical technologists," highlighting long-standing neglect of their professions.

Abdus Samad, president of the council, said the recruitment of medical technologists has remained frozen for over 14 years, leaving many qualified individuals unemployed. He added that many professionals have crossed the age limit for government jobs due to the prolonged suspension of hiring.

Samad said despite their qualifications, medical technologists face uncertainty, as the recruitment process initiated in 2013 remains stalled. He stressed the need for a separate directorate, which could address the profession's challenges and streamline recruitment.

The protesters also demanded recognition of diploma holders at the 10th grade in the government pay scale, the creation of 9th-grade positions for graduates, and the upgrading of Dhaka's Institute of Health Technology to a university.

They called for the establishment of a Medical Technology Council and a Diploma Medical Education Board to regulate the sector.

Md Ripon Shikder, general secretary of the council, said higher education in medical technology was introduced over two decades ago under public universities, but no government positions have been created for graduates.

He added that only 4,106 of the 5,975 sanctioned positions for medical technologists in government institutions are currently filled, leaving a critical gap in the workforce.

Citing World Health Organization standards, Shikdar said there should be five medical technologists and three nurses per doctor, underscoring the pressing need to fill vacancies and reform the sector.
